Faster training

Author

Marie-Hélène Burle

The training loop of the previous section is modern and complete, but it runs exactly as written: one Python-level operation at a time. This section covers the standard levers that make a working loop fast: torch.compile, reduced-precision matrix math, the profiler that tells you where the time actually goes, and the arithmetic that tells you whether a model fits on a GPU.

Setup

import time  # to time epochs

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset
from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT
from torchvision.transforms import v2 as T

The data pipeline is the canonical one of the course: training transforms with augmentation, batches of 64, four persistent workers. Only the training loader is needed here:

IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

train_tf = T.Compose([
    T.ToImage(),
    T.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    T.RandomVerticalFlip(),
    T.RandomRotation(90),
    T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    T.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD),
])

idx = torch.load("data/split.pt", weights_only=True)
train = Subset(EuroSAT(root="data", transform=train_tf), idx["train"])
train_loader = DataLoader(
    train, batch_size=64, num_workers=4, persistent_workers=True,
    pin_memory=torch.accelerator.is_available(),
)
print(len(train_loader), "batches")

And the model is the small CNN of the previous section, with its loss and optimizer. This page only times training steps, so the metrics, the schedule, and the early stopping are left out:

class Net(nn.Module):
    """A small CNN for 64x64 images and 10 classes."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(128, 10),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.layers(x)

model = Net().to(device)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))

A baseline epoch

Here is the timing harness for this page: one warmup epoch (worker startup, CUDA context, caches), then one timed epoch at steady state:

def timed_epoch(m):
    """Run one epoch of bare training steps on model m, return seconds."""
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for x, y in train_loader:
        x = x.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        y = y.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(m(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    torch.accelerator.synchronize()
    return time.perf_counter() - t0
timed_epoch(model)  # warmup
print(f"eager: {timed_epoch(model):4.1f} s")
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is eager PyTorch: each operation is launched one at a time, exactly as the code is written. On small models like ours, the accelerator spends much of each step waiting for the next kernel launch: the model is so small that its 95,000 parameters cannot keep the hardware busy.

torch.compile

torch.compile wraps a module so that its first call captures the operations into a graph, which is then compiled into fused kernels and optimized as a whole:

compiled = torch.compile(model)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • The return value is a drop-in replacement: call it, pass it to the profiling code below, everything works as before.
  • The wrapped model’s parameters are the same objects the optimizer already holds: no new optimizer needed.
  • Nothing happens yet: compilation is deferred to the first call.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
timed_epoch(compiled)  # first call: compiles
torch.accelerator.synchronize()
print(f"first epoch (with compilation): {time.perf_counter() - t0:4.1f} s")

Two things to read in these numbers:

  • The first epoch pays a one-time compilation cost, typically tens of seconds for a model this size. The compiled artifacts are cached on disk (under Triton’s cache directory), so a later process that compiles the same graph starts faster.
  • From the second epoch on, the compiled model runs the same training step faster than eager. How much faster varies a lot: our CNN interleaves convolutions with small elementwise operations, and fusing those helps, but the big convolutions were already well served by cuDNN. Models with more Python-level overhead (transformers are the classic) see larger gains.

What happens under the hood? Two things. First, TorchDynamo records the operations your Python code performs on the model into a graph (stopping at “graph breaks” it cannot handle, and compiling each fragment). Second, the Inductor backend generates optimized kernels for that graph: Triton kernels on GPUs. Fusing sequences of elementwise operations into one kernel is where much of the speedup comes from: fewer launches, and intermediate results stay in fast GPU memory.

Watch out for recompilations. A graph is compiled for the shapes it sees. Our training loader yields batches of shape (64, 3, 64, 64) all the way, except the last one, which has 32 images: the first epoch compiles the model twice. With many distinct shapes (variable sequence lengths, varying image sizes), torch.compile can spend its time recompiling instead of training. Two remedies: drop_last=True on the training loader (we met the option when counting batches), and torch.compile(model, dynamic=True) to compile shape-generic graphs.

torch.compile also takes a mode argument: the default balances compile time against speed, while mode="max-autotune" lets the compiler try more kernel variants at the cost of longer compilation. For a loop that runs for hours, a few extra minutes of compilation are a good trade.

TF32

The compute that dominates training is matrix multiplication, and GPUs have fast units for it. Since the Ampere generation (2020), NVIDIA GPUs can run float32 matrix products in TF32, a format that keeps float32’s range but carries only 10 bits of mantissa. The accuracy loss is invisible for deep learning, and the speedup on matmul-heavy workloads is substantial.

Format Sign Exponent Mantissa Notes
float32 1 8 23 the default dtype of training
TF32 1 8 10 float32 range, reduced precision, used internally by tensor cores
bfloat16 1 8 7 the autocast format of our loop

PyTorch lets you pick how float32 matmuls are allowed to degrade:

print(torch.get_float32_matmul_precision())
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[10], line 1
----> 1 print(torch.get_float32_matmul_precision())

NameError: name 'torch' is not defined

The default, "highest", never leaves float32. "high" allows TF32 (or bfloat16 on hardware without TF32), and "medium" allows bfloat16. Convolutions have a separate switch, torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32, which has been True by default for years.

torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")  # one line, usually near the top of a script

TF32 needs Ampere or newer. The RTX 2060 this page renders on is a Turing GPU: no TF32 units, so the setting changes nothing here, and our bf16 gate keeps autocast off for the same reason. On the cluster GPUs of the later sections, both switches open and the same code speeds up.

Profiling

Before optimizing anything longer than a page, measure. torch.profiler records what each part of a step costs: which kernels ran, for how long, on which device.

import os

from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile

os.environ["KINETO_LOG_LEVEL"] = "100"  # silence the profiler's own logging

x, y = next(iter(train_loader))
x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
for _ in range(3):  # warmup: the first step always runs extra one-time work
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

activities = [ProfilerActivity.CPU]
if device.type == "cuda":
    activities.append(ProfilerActivity.CUDA)
with profile(activities=activities, record_shapes=True) as prof:
    for _ in range(5):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

How to read the table:

  • Each row aggregates all calls to one operation. Self CPU/CUDA is the time spent in the operation itself; CPU total / CUDA total includes its children. Look at the self columns to find the actual hot spots.
  • Self CPU % often shows a large cudaLaunchKernel-ish share in small models: the CPU issuing work faster than the GPU? No: the CPU waiting to issue the next launch. That is the overhead torch.compile reduces.
  • CUDA total empty while CPU total is large marks code that runs on the CPU: a sign that something (data manipulation, a metric computed on CPU tensors) silently left the accelerator.

The table answers “which operation”; for “called from where”, export a trace and open it in a trace viewer:

prof.export_chrome_trace("trace.json")  # then open https://ui.perfetto.dev

The profiler only sees what runs inside its context: our snippet reuses one batch to keep the trace focused on compute, so the data pipeline of the DataLoaders section is invisible here. For a data-starved run, the diagnosis tools of that section (epoch times, nvidia-smi) come first.

The memory side

Speed is one constraint; memory (VRAM) is the other. Training a model keeps several copies of the parameters in GPU memory, and knowing their sizes tells you at a glance what fits.

For a model trained in float32 with an adaptive optimizer like AdamW:

def training_footprint(n_params):
    """Approximate VRAM for the learned state of a model in MiB."""
    per_param = (
        4  # weights
        + 4  # gradients
        + 4 + 4  # AdamW keeps two moments per parameter
    )
    return n_params * per_param / 2**20

n_ours = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"our CNN:        {n_ours:>10,} params  ~{training_footprint(n_ours):6.1f} MiB")

Two conclusions:

  • Both models fit easily in the 6 GiB of the laptop GPU this course renders on. Add activations (the intermediate results of the forward pass, which scale with batch size), and ResNet-18 training at batch 64 still stays in the neighbourhood of a couple of GiB.
  • The arithmetic explains when models stop fitting: a 7-billion-parameter model trained in float32 with AdamW needs about 104 GiB for weights, gradients, and moments alone, before a single activation. No single GPU holds that; splitting the training state across several of them is the topic of a later section.

To measure rather than estimate on a CUDA GPU, read the allocator’s high-water mark after a training step:

torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()  # then run one step
print(f"peak: {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**20:.0f} MiB")

Note that mixed precision does not halve this footprint: with autocast, weights, gradients, and optimizer state stay in float32; only the compute runs in bf16.

Where to start

In the order that pays off the soonest:

  1. Feed the accelerator (previous section): workers, prefetching, pinned memory. No code change in the model.
  2. torch.compile: one line, meaningful gains on most models, first-call compilation cost.
  3. Precision: TF32 where available, bf16 autocast otherwise (the gate of our loop).
  4. More hardware: when one GPU is genuinely not enough, the cluster sections take over.

And measure between steps: the profiler for compute, epoch times for the big picture.

Your turn:

Compile with mode="max-autotune" and compare the steady-state epoch time with the default mode. Then add drop_last=True to the training loader and check that the recompilation for the small final batch disappears from the first epoch.

  • Hint: max-autotune compiles for noticeably longer; watch the first epoch’s total time versus the second.
